resources.string: See the world through nature\'s eyes
Transforms camera sensor data into anatomically and physically accurate spectral simulations of animal photoreceptors, lenses, and retinal optics.

Dogs have two types of cone photoreceptors (S at 435nm, M/L at 555nm). They see the world in blue and yellow hues, are red-green color blind (deuteranopia), and have a reflective tapetum lucidum enhancing twilight sensitivity by 4–5x.
Red-Green Blind (Deuteranopia): Reds & greens appear yellow-brown
20/75 Visual Acuity: 3–4x blurrier than human 20/20 vision
Tapetum Lucidum: 4–5x light amplification in dark conditions

Deer possess dichromatic vision with cones peaking at 455nm (S-cone) and 537nm (M-cone). Lacking a UV filter in their lens, they perceive blue/UV light ~20x more prominently. With no red L-cones, hunter blaze orange appears as a dull, low-contrast brownish-gray.
20/60 Acuity & Horizontal Streak: Sharpest along the horizon
No UV Filter: Blue jeans & UV brighteners glow 20x brighter
Blaze Orange Camouflage: 537nm cone cutoff turns blaze orange into dull brown/gray
18x Twilight Vision: Horizontal tapetum maximizes dawn & dusk light
300° Panoramic FOV: Horizontal slit pupils with 50° cyclovergence rotation

Cats have a 25:1 rod-to-cone ratio optimized for twilight hunting. Their vertical slit pupils and huge retroreflective tapetum provide 6–8x night amplification. Colors appear soft and pastel with intense green-cyan night sensitivity.
25:1 Rod-to-Cone Ratio: High motion detection, pastel colors
Vertical Stenopaeic Slit Pupil: Pinpoint light control from bright sun to darkness
6–8x Night Vision: Massive tapetum lucidum reflection
Avian Tetrachromat with Oil Droplet Filters

Birds have four cone classes (UV/Violet ~380nm, Blue ~450nm, Green ~535nm, Red ~570nm) equipped with colored carotenoid oil droplets that act as sharp optical bandpass filters. They perceive a hyperspectral color gamut and possess ultra-sharp 20/5 visual acuity.
Tetrachromacy: 4 cone types perceiving ultraviolet plumage and trails
Carotenoid Oil Droplets: Sharpen wavelength separation for extreme color contrast
20/5 Visual Acuity: 4x sharper than human vision with deep dual foveas

Bees see ultraviolet (345nm), blue (440nm), and green (540nm), but are completely blind to red (which appears black). Their compound eye contains ~5000 hexagonal ommatidia facets, revealing hidden UV "nectar guides" on flower petals.
Red Blind: Long red wavelengths (>580nm) appear black
UV Nectar Guides: Petals show vibrant UV patterns guiding to nectar
Hexagonal Ommatidia: Mosaic compound eye resolution
Visual Dichromacy + Thermal IR Pit Organ

Pit vipers combine dichromatic optical vision with bilateral facial pit organs sensitive to long-wave thermal infrared (8–12µm). Neural processing in the optic tectum fuses optical imagery with a false-color thermal heat map of warm-blooded prey.
Thermal Pit Organs: Detects radiant infrared body heat at 8–12µm
Optic Tectum Fusion: Merges visual light and thermal heat maps
Dichromatic Background: Adapted for motion and nocturnal hunting
